cues.text: The Words at the Supper
On the night before he died, Christ took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and told his disciples this was his body.
He did the same with the cup, calling it his blood.
Matthew, Mark, and Luke all record the words, each writing independently, each preserving the same central claim.
This is among the most consistently attested episodes in the Gospels.

The wording varies slightly between the three accounts, as eyewitness testimony recorded by different hands naturally does, but the claim itself never softens into something merely symbolic in any of them.
Paul's Earlier Testimony
St.
Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians was written earlier than any of the four Gospels, likely around AD 54, only about two decades after the events it describes.
Paul tells the Corinthians he is passing on what he himself received directly from the Lord — language he elsewhere reserves for the Church's most essential, non-negotiable tradition.
His account of the Last Supper matches the Synoptic Gospels closely, giving the Church's central Eucharistic claim a written witness older than any surviving Gospel manuscript.
A Hard Saying in Capernaum
In the sixth chapter of John's Gospel, Christ tells a crowd in the synagogue at Capernaum that his flesh is true food and his blood true drink.
The listeners are visibly scandalized, asking how this man could possibly give them his flesh to eat.
Elsewhere in the Gospels, when a crowd misreads a hard teaching, Christ typically clarifies it privately for his disciples.
Here he does the opposite — he repeats the claim more forcefully rather than soften it.
John records that many of his disciples turned back after this and no longer accompanied him, and Christ lets them go rather than explain the words away.
Answerable for the Body and the Blood
Writing to the same Corinthians about receiving Communion carelessly, Paul warns that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup unworthily will have to answer for the body and blood of the Lord.
That is the language of a real offense against a real person, not merely a warning about mishandling a symbol.

Taken together, these four threads — the Supper narratives, Paul's early testimony, the Capernaum discourse, and Paul's warning about unworthy reception — form the biblical foundation beneath every account gathered elsewhere in this exhibition.
